config.rubric: A full answer explains that the count of Blocker findings isn't itself evidence of misuse — what matters is whether each one individually meets the strict definition, which the prompt states they do.

hints: The lesson's actual concern was 11 findings crammed into 'Critical' that didn't all meet the definition — not a specific count being inherently suspicious.
Ask whether each of the 6 was individually verified against the strict definition, which the prompt confirms.
A genuinely broken product could have many real blockers; the number itself proves nothing either way.
explanation: False. The lesson's actual point was that findings were being mislabelled Critical without meeting the strict definition — the fix was applying the definition precisely, not capping the count. If a product genuinely has 6 different, independently-verified points of complete task failure for different categories of users, all 6 deserve the Blocker rating; a large number of correctly-applied Blocker findings just means the product has many real blockers, which is itself important information, not evidence of a loosely-applied scale.

prompt: Sort each finding into 'Blocker (complete task failure for a category of user)' or 'Serious but completable.'

categories: Blocker (complete task failure for a category of user)

items.text: A file-upload control that only accepts drag-and-drop with no keyboard or click alternative, on a form that requires uploading a document to proceed
items.category: Blocker (complete task failure for a category of user)

items.text: A confusingly-worded error message that takes a screen reader user several attempts to understand, but eventually leads to a successful fix and submission
A live chat widget that traps keyboard focus with no Escape or reachable close control, on a page where the chat isn't required to complete any task
A CAPTCHA with no audio or alternative, the sole gate before an account password can be reset
items.category: Blocker (complete task failure for a category of user)

hints: Apply the strict test each time: can the affected user genuinely finish the task at all, through any sequence, however patient they are?
A keyboard trap on a non-essential widget is a real, serious finding, but doesn't block the actual task the page exists for.
A required upload with no alternative to drag-and-drop is a genuine full stop for keyboard-only or switch-access users.
explanation: The two Blocker items both represent genuine, total failure: no keyboard-only or switch-access path exists to upload the required document at all, and no path around the CAPTCHA exists to reset a password at all. The two 'serious but completable' items are both real, worth-fixing findings that a determined user can still push through — a confusing error eventually resolved, and a keyboard trap on a widget that isn't required for the actual task.

prompt: A Level AA finding (a heading structure that skips from h1 to h4) is present on one internal, rarely-used documentation page. Should its severity automatically be Medium because AA maps to Medium?

options.text: Yes — Level AA criteria should always be rated Medium for consistency
No — severity should be assessed on this specific instance's actual impact, frequency and workaround, independent of its conformance level
Yes, but only because heading structure specifically always maps to Medium
No severity rating is needed for Level AA findings

hints: Recall the core lesson: conformance level and severity are independent axes.
A skipped heading level on a rarely-used page is likely to have quite low real-world impact — that's worth actually assessing, not assuming from the criterion.
The finding still needs a severity rating; the question is how it should be derived.
explanation: Conformance level and severity are independent, and defaulting to a fixed mapping from one to the other skips the actual judgement severity requires. This specific instance — a heading-structure issue on a rarely-used internal page — likely warrants a genuinely low severity based on its actual impact and frequency, arrived at by assessing this instance directly, not by reading it off the AA label.

prompt: Match each scenario to whether grouping under one root-cause finding is justified or not.

pairs.left: 30 buttons across the site all built from the same shared Button component, all missing focus styles due to one CSS rule
pairs.right: Justified — verified shared cause, one fix location

pairs.left: 12 forms with similar-looking validation errors, built by three different teams using three unrelated frameworks over several years
pairs.right: Not justified — surface resemblance without a verified shared cause

pairs.left: 8 instances of the exact same date picker component, confirmed via the codebase to all import from one shared module
pairs.right: Justified — verified shared cause, one fix location

pairs.left: 5 pages with contrast issues on different, unrelated custom-colored text elements with no shared style source
pairs.right: Not justified — surface resemblance without a verified shared cause

hints: The test each time is whether a fix at one location would actually resolve every instance.
Similar-looking symptoms built by different teams or frameworks are the exact case this module warns against grouping.
A confirmed shared import or shared CSS rule is real evidence of shared cause, not just an assumption.
explanation: Grouping is justified only where the shared cause is actually verified — a confirmed shared component import, or one shared CSS rule affecting every instance — because in both cases, fixing the one source genuinely resolves every listed instance. Where the resemblance is only surface-level (different teams, different frameworks, different unrelated style sources), grouping would misrepresent unrelated defects as one bug and risks the same 'silently assumed covered, actually never fixed' failure from earlier in this module.

prompt: A stakeholder says, in a review call: 'I get that it's a real bug, but Critical feels dramatic for a dropdown.' The finding: a custom dropdown for selecting insurance plan type has no keyboard operability at all — can't be opened, navigated, or selected with a keyboard, on the one required field standing between a user and completing a mandatory benefits enrollment. Write your response.
hints: Separate the general category ('a dropdown') from what makes this specific instance meet the Blocker bar.
Walk through impact, frequency and workaround explicitly, the same way as the earlier contrast example.
Stay on the finding's mechanism, not on defending the word 'Critical' as a label.
explanation: A strong response does the same separation as the earlier contrast drill: 'A dropdown in general, sure, wouldn't usually be Critical — this one is, because of what it specifically blocks. Impact: total — there's no keyboard way to open, navigate, or select an option in this control at all, and it's the one required field standing between a keyboard-only user and completing mandatory enrollment. Frequency: every keyboard-only user attempting enrollment hits this exact wall. Workaround: none — there's no alternative input method offered anywhere on the page. If there were a text-input fallback, or if this were an optional field, I'd rate it lower. Happy to demo the exact repro if that helps.' This keeps the conversation on the specific mechanism (total block, mandatory field, no fallback) rather than defending the label in the abstract.

prompt: A product owner disputes a rating in a review call. Put these steps in the order you'd actually take to handle it well.

items: Listen fully to what specifically is being disputed, rather than assuming you already know
Determine whether any new, verifiable fact about impact, frequency, or workaround has actually been introduced
If no new fact was introduced, calmly restate the original framework-based reasoning for the specific finding
If a genuine new fact was introduced, re-derive the rating honestly from the updated facts
Document whichever outcome occurred — held or revised — and the specific reason, in the report itself

hints: You can't correctly classify the dispute as 'new fact' or 'no new fact' without first actually listening to what's being said.
The response (restate vs. revise) depends entirely on the outcome of that classification.
Documenting the reasoning afterward matters for both outcomes, not just a revision — a held rating benefits from a documented reason too.
explanation: This sequence prevents both failure modes covered in this module's final lesson: reacting defensively or conceding before actually listening skips the step that determines which response is even appropriate, and failing to document the outcome either way leaves no record for the next person who reads the report and wonders why a rating is what it is, or whether it was ever actually challenged.

prompt: 45 instances of a missing accessible name on an icon button are traced to one shared IconButton component. The finding is written as one root-cause item naming the component and listing all 45 instances. Three weeks later, only 40 of the 45 show the fix. What should have been checked, and when?

options.text: Nothing — since the fix was made at the component level, all 45 should be assumed fixed automatically
The full list of all 45 instances should have been explicitly re-checked after the fix shipped, rather than assuming the component-level change reached every one of them
The finding should never have been grouped into one root cause in the first place
Only the highest-severity instance among the 45 needed re-checking

hints: Recall the forked-component-version example from this module — a component-level fix doesn't automatically guarantee it reached every instance.
The grouping itself was fine, assuming the shared cause was genuinely verified — this is about the verification step after the fix.
Spot-checking one instance wouldn't have caught the 5 that didn't get the fix.
explanation: This is the exact scenario the lesson's second pod covers: a component-level fix doesn't automatically guarantee it reached every listed instance — some pages may pull from a forked, cached, or otherwise divergent version. The full instance list compiled when the finding was first written needs to be explicitly re-checked during retest, not assumed complete because the shared source was updated — which is exactly how the 5 unfixed instances were caught here, three weeks late instead of immediately.

prompt: An audit report's findings section is ordered exactly by the sequence testing happened to occur in — the homepage first (tested on day one), then the checkout flow (tested on day four), then a component library review (tested on day nine), regardless of severity. What's the actual problem with this ordering?

options.text: It's fine — chronological order is the most honest, unbiased way to present findings
It reflects the auditor's own process rather than what either an executive or a developer reader actually needs first — the most severe findings could be buried on page 60
Testing order and severity always happen to align anyway, so it doesn't matter in practice
Nothing is wrong, as long as a table of contents exists

hints: Ask what an executive reader, specifically, needs to see first — and whether that's guaranteed to be whatever was tested first.
There's no reason testing order and severity would correlate at all — day one's page could easily have only minor findings while day nine's component review turns up a blocker.
A table of contents helps navigation, but doesn't fix a structure that buries the most important content deep in the document by default.
explanation: Chronological ordering reflects nothing about what matters to a reader — it's simply an artefact of which page happened to get tested first. There's no reason to expect the most severe findings to cluster near the front under this ordering; a genuine blocker discovered on day nine could sit on page 60, while day one's minor cosmetic findings occupy the first ten pages. A table of contents helps someone navigate to a specific section if they already know it exists, but doesn't solve the more basic problem that the document's own order doesn't reflect what's actually most important.

prompt: An auditor writes the report's methodology section from memory, several weeks after testing concluded, rather than referring back to the original scope document.

config.statement: This is fine as long as the auditor remembers the general shape of what was tested — exact precision in the methodology section isn't important.
config.rubric: A full answer explains that the methodology section should accurately reflect what was actually tested (sample, matrix, exclusions), and that the original scope document — kept accurate throughout the engagement per the earlier module — is the reliable source for this, not memory reconstructed weeks later.

hints: Consider what happens if memory and the actual scope document disagree about what was or wasn't tested.
The methodology section is a factual claim about what was done — a client could reasonably rely on it being accurate.
This directly connects to why the earlier module emphasised keeping the scope document updated as facts changed during the engagement.
explanation: False. The methodology section makes a specific factual claim about what was and wasn't tested — a client may rely on it when deciding what to do about anything not covered. Reconstructing it from memory weeks later risks exactly the kind of inaccuracy (misremembering which browser combinations were actually used, forgetting an exclusion that was agreed to mid-engagement) that an accurate, maintained scope document exists to prevent. The methodology section should be built from that document directly, not from recollection.

prompt: A colleague asks why every single finding in your reports uses the identical field order (title, severity, citation, location, impact, recommendation) even when a particular finding would read more naturally as a flowing paragraph. Write your answer.
hints: Think about the fifteenth finding in the report, not just the first one.
A reader who's learned the format from earlier findings can scan later ones far faster.
Naturalness for a single finding read in isolation isn't the same goal as scannability across a whole report.
explanation: A strong answer names the actual trade-off directly: a single finding read in isolation might read slightly more naturally as free-flowing prose, but a report has fifteen, forty, or a hundred findings, read by people who need to scan for specific ones — a developer checking whether their component appears anywhere, an executive triaging by severity. Once a reader has seen the format in the first finding, every subsequent one becomes scannable: they know exactly where to look for severity, or location, without reading the whole entry. That predictability is worth more, across a whole report, than any one finding reading slightly more elegantly on its own — consistency is itself a feature for the reader, not a stylistic compromise.

prompt: A finding states: 'The search results page's filter checkboxes are missing labels. WCAG 4.1.2. Medium. Screen reader users can't tell what each filter does when navigating by form controls, hearing only "checkbox, not checked" for all twelve filters with no way to distinguish them. Add a visible label or aria-label naming each specific filter (e.g. "In stock," "Free shipping") to each checkbox.' Which of the four elements (what/where/who/what-to-do) is this finding missing, if any?

options.text: It's missing 'where' — no specific page or component is named
Nothing is missing — all four elements are present and specific
It's missing 'who' — no specific user category is named
It's missing 'what to do' — no concrete recommendation is given

hints: Check each of the four elements against the finding text directly.
'Search results page's filter checkboxes' is a specific location; 'screen reader users' is a specific category; the recommendation names exactly what to add.
This finding is written as a positive example, not a flawed one — check whether it actually meets the bar rather than assuming a gap exists.
explanation: This finding is complete: what (missing labels, and the specific resulting announcement), where (the search results page's filter checkboxes, specifically twelve of them), who (screen reader users navigating by form controls, unable to distinguish the filters), and what to do (add a specific label or aria-label per checkbox, with concrete examples). It's a usable model of what all four elements looks like written out explicitly, rather than a flawed example to critique.

prompt: Rewrite this generic impact statement into a specific one: 'This affects users with disabilities.' The finding it belongs to: a 'Load more results' button that, when activated, adds new items to the page but never moves or announces focus, so a screen reader user who activates it has no way of knowing new content appeared, or where to find it, without manually searching the whole page again.
hints: Name the specific category of user (screen reader users, not 'users with disabilities' broadly).
State the specific task and the specific mechanism of the barrier — what exactly can't they do, and why.
Check: would this sentence be obviously wrong if pasted onto a completely different finding?
explanation: A specific version: 'Screen reader users who activate "Load more results" receive no indication that new content has been added and no way to locate it without manually re-exploring the entire page from the top — effectively making incremental loading invisible to them, and turning a one-click action into a full page re-search.' This names the specific category (screen reader users), the specific task (finding newly-loaded content), and the specific mechanism (no focus movement or announcement on load) — this sentence would be visibly wrong if pasted onto an unrelated finding, which is the actual test of whether it's specific enough.

prompt: An auditor writes exact, specific-looking code into a recommendation for a live-region announcement, without having seen the client's actual component source code — reasoning that a specific-looking snippet demonstrates more expertise than a general description.

config.statement: Including specific code the auditor hasn't verified against the real codebase is a reasonable way to demonstrate expertise and give the developer a head start.
config.rubric: A full answer explains that unverified specific code risks being actively wrong for the real codebase, which can mislead or confuse a developer more than an honest, outcome-focused description would, and that this is a real cost the appearance of expertise doesn't offset.

hints: Weigh the actual risk: what happens if the guessed code doesn't match the real structure at all?
A developer following incorrect specific code can lose more time than one working from an accurate general description.
The appearance of expertise isn't the same as the recommendation actually being correct and usable.
explanation: False. Specific-looking code that turns out not to match the real codebase's structure can actively mislead a developer — they might spend time trying to make an inapplicable snippet work, or lose trust in the rest of the report once they discover it was guessed rather than verified. An honest, outcome-focused recommendation ('the confirmation needs to be announced via a live region or your framework's equivalent mechanism — happy to review the actual markup') is more genuinely useful than confident-looking code that might be wrong, even though it looks less impressively specific on the page.

prompt: A recommendation reads only: 'Make this more accessible.' What's the actual problem with this, given the earlier lesson's argument against over-specific unverified code?

options.text: Nothing — this is exactly the right level of caution, since it avoids guessing at the codebase entirely
It goes too far in the opposite direction — naming no outcome and no technique at all leaves a developer with nothing concrete to act on, which is a different but equally real failure
It should be replaced with exact code regardless of whether the codebase has been inspected
This is fine as long as a WCAG citation is attached elsewhere in the finding

hints: The lesson's actual point is about finding the right middle ground, not about avoiding specificity altogether.
A recommendation needs to name the outcome precisely, even if it stops short of exact, unverified code.
A citation alone doesn't tell a developer what needs to change.
explanation: 'Make this more accessible' avoids the over-specification problem by avoiding specificity of any kind — but that swings too far the other way, leaving a developer with no concrete outcome to aim for at all. The actual target is naming precisely what needs to be true when the fix is done (the outcome) and the general technique or pattern that achieves it, without dictating exact, unverified syntax — not choosing between 'too specific' and 'not specific at all' as the only two options.

prompt: Sort each recommendation approach into 'safe to show as real code (near-universal technique)' or 'safer to describe as an outcome (codebase-dependent).'

categories: Safe to show as real code (near-universal technique)
Safer to describe as an outcome (codebase-dependent)

items.text: The standard visually-hidden-but-focusable CSS pattern for a skip link
items.category: Safe to show as real code (near-universal technique)

items.text: The exact way a specific React component's internal state should trigger an accessible live-region announcement
items.category: Safer to describe as an outcome (codebase-dependent)

items.text: The standard HTML attribute and value for marking a required form field (aria-required="true" or the required attribute)
items.category: Safe to show as real code (near-universal technique)

items.text: The exact class names and DOM structure a specific design system's modal component should use to trap focus correctly
items.category: Safer to describe as an outcome (codebase-dependent)

hints: Ask, for each: does the correct implementation depend on knowing this specific codebase's internal structure, or is it close to identical everywhere?
A raw HTML attribute or a well-known CSS pattern doesn't depend on a specific framework's internals.
Anything referencing a specific component's internal state, class names, or DOM structure requires actually having seen that code.
explanation: The dividing line is whether the correct implementation depends on knowing this specific codebase's internal structure. The skip-link CSS pattern and the standard HTML attribute for required fields are close to identical regardless of framework or codebase — safe to show as real, specific code. The React component's internal state-to-announcement wiring and a specific design system's exact class names and DOM structure both genuinely depend on code the auditor hasn't inspected — safer to describe as an outcome and a general technique, with an offer to review the real implementation.

prompt: An audit found 1 genuine Blocker finding among 30 total. The executive summary states: 'Testing identified 30 findings across the product. Full details, including one finding rated Blocker severity affecting the account-deletion flow, are provided in the findings section below, ordered by severity.' Is this executive summary honest?

options.text: No — it should have opened with reassuring language about the other 29 findings first
Yes — it states the existence and nature of the Blocker finding plainly in the summary itself, rather than requiring the reader to discover it only by reading further
No — a Blocker finding should never be mentioned in an executive summary, only in the detailed findings section
It can't be judged as honest or dishonest without knowing the exact WCAG citation

hints: Check whether a reader who stops after the summary alone would still know the most consequential fact.
This is a positive example — check whether it actually meets the standard rather than assuming a flaw exists.
The WCAG citation isn't what determines whether a summary is honest about severity.
explanation: This is honest: a reader who reads only the executive summary and nothing else still learns that a genuine Blocker exists and roughly what it affects, which is exactly the information the earlier dishonest-by-omission example withheld. It doesn't need to open with reassurance about the other 29 findings, and burying the Blocker finding entirely in a later section — rather than naming it plainly in the summary — would repeat the exact failure this lesson's first pod describes, just in a different arrangement.

prompt: Write a two-to-three sentence executive summary opening for an audit that found 0 Blocker findings, 1 High-severity finding (a low-contrast primary button on the pricing page, genuinely hard to locate for users with low vision, though the page remains navigable), and 22 Moderate/Low findings.
hints: State plainly that no blockers were found, but don't let that read as 'nothing to see here' — the 1 High finding still deserves to be named specifically.
Avoid alarmist language that isn't proportionate to a genuinely moderate overall picture.
Give a proportionate, honest practical read of what this distribution actually means to act on.
explanation: A strong version: 'Testing found no findings that block task completion outright. One High-severity finding — a low-contrast primary call-to-action button on the pricing page — makes a key action genuinely hard to locate for users with low vision and is worth prioritising soon, though the page remains navigable. The remaining 22 findings are Moderate or Low severity and represent real, worthwhile improvements rather than urgent risks.' This is honest in both directions: it doesn't inflate a genuinely moderate picture into alarming language, and it doesn't let the reassuring absence of Blockers erase the one finding that does deserve real, prompt attention.

prompt: Rewrite this finding to frame it on the system rather than on individuals, while keeping every underlying fact and the severity rating identical: 'Whoever built this modal clearly didn't test it with a keyboard at all — focus isn't trapped correctly and Escape doesn't close it. This kind of basic oversight shouldn't make it to production.'
hints: Remove language that judges a person's competence or effort ('clearly didn't,' 'basic oversight').
Describe the modal's current behaviour and what it needs to do instead, as a system fact.
Consider recommending a process fix (a keyboard-testing step) alongside the specific instance fix, the same pattern as the alt-text example.
explanation: A system-framed version: 'The modal does not currently trap keyboard focus correctly, and the Escape key does not close it — a keyboard-only user who opens this modal cannot reliably navigate within it or exit it. Recommend adding keyboard interaction testing (focus trapping and Escape-to-close specifically) to the component's testing checklist, alongside fixing this instance.' This keeps the exact same facts and the same severity, removes every phrase that judges a person ('whoever built this,' 'clearly didn't,' 'basic oversight,' 'shouldn't make it to production'), and adds a concrete process recommendation that prevents recurrence — which is a more useful outcome than an accusation, even one aimed at nobody in particular.

prompt: An auditor softens a genuine Blocker-severity finding's rating down to Medium specifically because they're worried the development team will feel demoralised by a harsh-sounding rating.

config.statement: This is a reasonable, kind thing to do, and consistent with this lesson's guidance about not shaming the team who wrote the code.
config.rubric: A full answer distinguishes kindness in framing/language (which this lesson recommends) from dishonesty in the severity rating itself (which it explicitly does not recommend, and which repeats the dishonest-by-omission failure from the previous lesson).

hints: This lesson's actual guidance is about the language surrounding a finding, not about the accuracy of its severity rating.
Recall the previous lesson's point about executive summaries — the same discipline about honest severity applies at the individual-finding level too.
Ask what the actual cost is if the team never learns this is genuinely a Blocker.
explanation: False. This lesson's guidance is specifically about framing language — describing a system gap rather than a personal failing — not about the accuracy of the severity rating, which needs to stay honest regardless of tone. Softening a genuine Blocker to Medium to spare feelings misrepresents the real, verified impact (complete task failure for a category of users) and risks the team deprioritising something that genuinely needs urgent attention — the same dishonesty-by-omission problem from the executive summary lesson, just applied to one finding instead of the whole report. Kindness belongs in the words used to describe the finding, never in the number attached to it.

prompt: A finding reads: 'Icon buttons throughout the app lack labels.' Which single addition would most improve it first?

options.text: A severity rating alone, with nothing else changed
A specific instance count and location — which icon buttons, on which screens, or a confirmed shared component with a full instance list
A joke to lighten the tone
Removing the word 'throughout,' since it sounds exaggerated

hints: Recall the root-cause instance-list discipline from the previous module — 'throughout the app' with no specifics is the vague version of that same gap.
'Where' is one of the four required elements, and this finding doesn't have it in usable form.
A severity rating alone doesn't fix the finding's actual missing content.
explanation: 'Throughout the app' names no specific location at all — a developer can't act on it without first doing their own investigation to find every instance, which is exactly the job a finding is supposed to have already done. Naming the specific instances (or confirming a shared component and listing every instance of it, per the root-cause discipline from the severity module) turns a vague impression into something actionable — this is a bigger fix than a severity rating, which doesn't address the underlying gap at all.

prompt: A recommendation reads: 'Ensure the modal component properly manages focus according to WAI-ARIA authoring practices for dialogs.'

config.statement: This recommendation is specific enough to act on, since it names a concrete standard (WAI-ARIA authoring practices) to follow.
config.rubric: A full answer explains that naming a standard to follow isn't the same as stating the specific outcome needed for this specific finding — a developer still has to go read and interpret the entire referenced document to figure out what 'properly manages focus' actually requires here.

hints: Ask what a developer would actually have to do next, having read only this sentence.
Naming a whole external standard to consult isn't the same as stating the specific outcome for this specific modal.
Compare this to the earlier lesson's better version, which named the specific behaviours needed (focus trapped, Escape closes it).
explanation: False. Citing a standard by name shifts the actual work of figuring out what's needed onto the developer, who now has to go read the entire WAI-ARIA authoring practices document and work out which parts apply to this specific modal. A genuinely actionable recommendation states the specific outcome directly — e.g. 'focus should be trapped within the modal while open, and Escape should close it and return focus to the trigger element' — which is exactly what the referenced standard would eventually tell them, done for them instead of left as homework.

prompt: Sort each phrase into 'system-framed' or 'person-framed (blame-coded).'

items.text: 'The image-upload workflow does not currently require alt text as a step'
'Whoever built this obviously skipped basic testing'
'This is a common gap in components that started as click-only prototypes'
'This carelessness reflects poorly on the team's QA process'

hints: Ask whether the phrase describes a process/pattern or judges a person's competence and effort.
'Doesn't currently require' and 'a common gap in this kind of component' both describe a system state, not a person.
'Obviously skipped' and 'carelessness' both directly judge the people involved.
explanation: The system-framed phrases describe a process gap or a known, common pattern without attributing it to anyone's competence or effort — they'd read the same regardless of who wrote the original code. The person-framed phrases explicitly judge the people involved ('obviously skipped,' 'carelessness'), which is exactly the language this module's final lesson recommends replacing, even when the underlying fact being described is accurate.

prompt: Put these sections in the order a report structure built for actual post-delivery use — not chronological testing order — should present them.

items: Executive summary
Methodology and scope
Findings, grouped by severity (highest first)
Technical appendix (full environment logs, raw scan output)

hints: An executive reader needs the headline before anything else, including before methodology.
Methodology grounds the findings that follow, so it belongs before them, not buried after.
The most detailed, least-often-needed material belongs last, available but not in the way of the main content.
explanation: This ordering front-loads what an executive reader needs immediately (the summary), grounds the findings in what was actually tested before presenting them (methodology), surfaces the most consequential content in a scannable, severity-first order (findings), and keeps the rarely-needed deep technical detail available but out of the main flow (appendix) — the structure this module's first lesson argues for, built around how the report will actually be used rather than the order testing happened to occur in.

prompt: Match each flawed finding element to the specific fix it needs.

pairs.left: 'This affects users with disabilities' (identical text pasted onto every finding in the report)
pairs.right: Replace with a specific task, mechanism, and user category unique to this finding

pairs.left: A recommendation with exact class names and DOM structure for a codebase the auditor never inspected
pairs.right: Replace with the outcome needed and a general technique, offering to review the actual code

pairs.left: 'The vast majority of findings were Medium or below' as the summary's headline, with 3 Blocker findings mentioned nowhere in it
pairs.right: State the Blocker findings plainly in the summary itself, not only in the detailed findings section

pairs.left: 'This carelessness reflects poorly on the QA process' attached to an accurate finding
pairs.right: Reframe on the system/pattern; keep the severity rating and underlying facts unchanged

hints: Each fix targets the specific gap in its paired flaw, without changing the underlying accurate facts.
The severity rating and the language around it are two separate things — only one of them should ever change to fix a tone problem.
A generic sentence needs specificity; over-specific unverified code needs generality; a buried headline needs foregrounding; blame-coded language needs reframing.
explanation: Each pairing applies the module's actual fix, not a generic 'make it better': a generic impact statement gets replaced with specifics unique to the finding; unverified specific code gets replaced with an honest outcome-and-technique description; a buried headline finding gets moved into the summary itself, stated plainly; and blame-coded language gets reframed onto the system while the severity rating and facts stay exactly as accurate as they were — kindness in language, never in the number.

prompt: Rewrite this finding to include all four required elements (what/where/who/what-to-do): 'Forms are hard to use with a screen reader. Needs work.'
hints: This finding is currently vague enough that you'll need to invent a plausible, specific version — state your assumptions if needed.
Name a specific form, a specific mechanism, a specific affected category, and a specific action.
This is a realistic example of the vaguest kind of finding a report should never actually contain.
explanation: A strong rewrite invents specific, plausible detail rather than staying vague, e.g.: 'What: the newsletter signup form's email field shows an inline validation error on blur, but the error text is not associated with the field via aria-describedby, so screen reader users aren't told what's wrong when they tab away from an invalid entry. Where: the newsletter signup form, present in the site footer on every page. Who: screen reader users who mistype their email address receive no explanation of the error and may resubmit repeatedly without understanding why it fails. What to do: associate the visible error text with the input using aria-describedby (or an equivalent live-region announcement) so it's read out when the error appears.' The exercise is really about demonstrating the pattern (what/where/who/what-to-do, each explicit) on a realistically vague starting point, not about a single correct answer.

prompt: An executive summary for an audit with 0 Blocker and 0 High findings, but 55 Moderate findings clustered heavily around one specific, high-traffic checkout journey, states only: 'No critical issues were found.' Is this honest?

options.text: Yes — since there are genuinely no Blocker findings, this is a completely accurate summary
No — it's technically true but omits that 55 real findings cluster around one high-traffic journey, which a reader deserves to know even without a top-severity finding present
No, because Moderate findings should never be mentioned in an executive summary at all
Yes, as long as the findings section lists all 55 in detail

hints: Recall this lesson's core point: individually true statements can still mislead by omission.
55 findings clustered around one high-traffic journey is a real, important pattern a summary reader deserves to know about.
Whether the details exist later in the report doesn't excuse a summary that gives a misleadingly thin impression on its own.
explanation: 'No critical issues were found' is technically true but tells a reader almost nothing about the real shape of the audit's findings — 55 Moderate findings concentrated on the single highest-traffic journey is a genuinely important pattern, even without a top-severity finding attached to it, and a summary reader deserves to know that shape exists rather than walking away with an impression close to 'nothing much was found.' This is the same dishonesty-by-omission mechanism as the lesson's opening example, just without a Blocker finding involved.

prompt: Rewrite this finding to remove blame-coded language while keeping every fact and the severity rating unchanged: 'The team clearly rushed this feature — the color contrast on the 'Buy now' button fails WCAG entirely, which is inexcusable for something this central to the product. Severity: High.'
hints: Keep 'Severity: High' exactly as is — this isn't about softening the rating.
Remove language judging the team's effort or process ('clearly rushed,' 'inexcusable') and replace with a description of the actual defect.
Consider whether a process-level recommendation adds real value alongside fixing this instance.
explanation: A system-framed version: 'The "Buy now" button's text color fails WCAG contrast requirements against its background (measured at approximately 2.1:1, against a 4.5:1 requirement for this text size). Given this is the primary purchase call-to-action, users with low vision may struggle to locate or confirm the correct button. Severity: High. Recommend correcting the button's color values, and adding a contrast check to the design review step for any new primary call-to-action component going forward.' This keeps High severity and every underlying fact intact, states the actual measurement rather than a vague accusation, and replaces 'clearly rushed' and 'inexcusable' with a description of the defect and a system-level process recommendation.
